title: Consumer Faith and the Communal Church: How We Forgot to Make Disciples
subtitle: Somewhere along the way the church stopped being a body and started being a vendor, and the Christian stopped being a disciple and started being a customer. This is the story of how American individualism and consumerism gutted disciple-making, why the ancient church that turned an empire upside down knew nothing of attending without belonging, and how the recovery of the table-shaped, one-another, ordinary-believer church is the recovery of disciple-making itself.

parts.title: The Church You Attend and Never Belong To
parts.body:
You go to church. You have gone for years, maybe for your whole life, and if someone asked you would say without hesitation that it matters to you. And yet here is a question you have learned not to ask out loud. After all those Sundays, who actually knows you. Not your name on a directory. Not the people who shake your hand at the door. Who has been in your kitchen, watched you lose your temper, heard the thing you are ashamed of, and stayed. For many of us the honest answer is no one, and we have made our peace with that, because the kind of church we know was never built to produce it.

We were trained, without anyone ever saying it, to treat the church the way we treat everything else in American life, as a provider of a service we consume. We attend. We evaluate. We compare the music here to the music there, the preaching, the programs, the parking, the children's wing, the coffee. We speak, without embarrassment, of church shopping, as though we were comparing vendors, and we are. We arrive, we receive, we leave, and the entire transaction can be completed without anyone knowing whether we are walking through a divorce or a crisis of faith or the best year of our lives. The building is full and the people inside it are strangers.

And so a strange thing has happened to a great many sincere believers. We have sat under good preaching for twenty years and are not noticeably more like Jesus than we were at the start. We can summarize the sermon and have not been formed by it. We know more than our grandparents did and obey less. We are, many of us, well-informed and unchanged, regular attenders who have never been discipled, because the thing we have been attending was never designed to disciple us. It was designed to gather us, hold our attention for an hour, and send us home unbothered. I have built services like that. I have measured a Sunday by the count and the comments and gone home content, and it has taken me years to feel the weight of what that meant.

Let me name the thing plainly. The problem is not that you are a bad Christian. The problem is that you have been handed a counterfeit of the thing, a private, individual, consuming Christianity that the New Testament would not recognize, and you have been doing it faithfully. You were promised that you could follow Jesus essentially alone, attend without belonging, believe without being known, and grow without being shared with, and it is not working, and it was never going to work. The church was never a vendor. It was a body. And a body part cannot live cut off from the body, no matter how good the service it receives.

parts.title: What Consumer Faith Cannot Do
parts.body:
The stakes begin with a quiet catastrophe we have been slow to name. The American church, by most measures of activity, has been busy and well-resourced for a century, and it has produced crowds of people who attend and a shortage of people who are formed. We built bigger rooms and better production and easier on-ramps, and we got bigger crowds and thinner Christians, and we kept assuming the answer was a better service when the problem was the service itself. You cannot consume your way into the character of Christ. Formation is not a product to be delivered to a passive recipient. It is a life shared in a body over time, and a consumer in a chair is the one posture in which it cannot happen.

Consider what consumer faith structurally cannot do. It cannot obey the one-another commands, the fifty-some times the New Testament tells Christians to love one another, bear one another's burdens, confess to one another, admonish one another, because every one of them requires a particular set of people who know you, and the consumer has traded the particular people for the anonymous crowd. It cannot produce repentance, because repentance needs someone close enough to name the sin and loved enough to be heard. It cannot carry you through suffering, because the people in the next row do not know you are suffering. The consumer church can deliver content to a stranger. It cannot do the actual work the New Testament assigns to the church, because that work runs entirely on being known, and being known is the one thing the consumer has arranged to avoid.

The stakes sharpen in a post-Christian America, where the old crowd is melting away in real time and the consumer model is melting with it. For decades the religious marketplace rewarded the church that competed best for the consumer, and a generation learned that church is a thing you select and discard like any other preference. Now the selecting generation is selecting nothing, walking away without drama, and we are stunned, but we should not be. We taught them that church was a vendor of religious goods, and they have simply found vendors they prefer, or decided they need none. You cannot disciple a culture out of a consumer faith using a more attractive consumer faith. The thing that is collapsing is the thing we built, and no improvement to it will save it.

And the stakes are generational and missional at once. A faith that is consumed cannot be reproduced, because the consumer learns that Christianity requires an institution, a professional, a building, a production he could never supply, and so the chain ends with him. But a faith that is shared in a body teaches every ordinary believer that they already possess everything disciple-making requires, a life, a table, a few people, the Spirit of God, and so they go and give it away. This is the difference between a church that maintains a crowd and a church that fills a city. The early Christians had no buildings, no clergy class as we know it, no programs, and no consumers, and they turned the Roman Empire upside down. We have all of those things, and we are shrinking. The connection is not an accident.

parts.title: The Body That Has No Spectators
parts.body:
Open the New Testament looking for a consumer Christian and you will not find one. You will find a body. Paul reaches for the image again and again because no other picture will carry the truth, that the church is not a collection of individuals who share a preference but a single living organism in which the parts cannot be detached without death. The eye cannot say to the hand I have no need of you. If one member suffers, all suffer together. If one is honored, all rejoice. There is no such thing in Paul's mind as a Christian who belongs to Christ and not to the others, because to be joined to the head is to be joined to the body, and a hand that imagines it can live in a drawer by itself has misunderstood what a hand is.

Look at how the church was born, because the shape it took on the first day is the shape it was meant to keep. After Pentecost, Luke says, the believers devoted themselves to the apostles teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. They were together and had all things in common. Day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts. This was not a service they attended. It was a life they shared, in homes, around tables, daily, with their possessions held loosely enough that no one among them was in need. The church did not have a fellowship hour. It was fellowship, a common life so thick and so visible that Luke says the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved. The growth was not a program. It was the overflow of a body that had become a family.

Luke returns to it in the fourth chapter and presses harder. The full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but they had everything in common. There was not a needy person among them. This is the most radical economic arrangement in the ancient world, and it grew not from a policy but from a conviction, that they were no longer a crowd of individuals but one body, and a body does not let one of its members starve while another is full. Whatever else this passage means, it cannot mean less than this, that the first Christians understood belonging to the church to lay an absolute claim on their lives, their homes, their money, and their time, the kind of claim a consumer never lets a vendor make.

And then there are the one-another commands, scattered across the letters like the load-bearing beams of a house. Love one another. Bear one another's burdens. Confess your sins to one another. Forgive one another. Encourage one another and build one another up. Admonish one another. Be kind to one another. Welcome one another. Bear with one another. Submit to one another. Spur one another on toward love and good deeds. Do not neglect to meet together, the writer to the Hebrews pleads, as is the habit of some. Read them all in a row and a single fact becomes inescapable. None of them can be obeyed by a Christian alone in a crowd. Every one requires the others, named and known, close enough to carry and be carried. The Christian life as the New Testament describes it is not a private transaction between an individual and God. It is a shared life in a body, and the one-anothers are simply the description of what that body does.

This is how Jesus himself made disciples, and it is the pattern the church inherited. He did not gather an audience and address it weekly. He called twelve men to be with him, Mark says, and then he shared three years of ordinary life with them, ate with them, walked with them, let them watch him handle the crowd and the storm and the cross, and formed them not by transferring information but by sharing a life. When he gave them the deepest meaning of his death he did not write them a treatise. He gave them a meal and said do this in remembrance of me. The whole of it ran on proximity, on being together, on the table and the road, and the church that came after simply kept doing what it had watched him do. There were no spectators in the upper room. There is no room in the body of Christ for a spectator now.

parts.title: How the Ancient Church Made Disciples Without a Program
parts.body:
Before the church had a single building of its own, it had households, and the household was where everything happened. For nearly three centuries the church met in homes, and the home set the scale of the whole enterprise. There was no platform separating a performer from an audience, no anonymity to hide in, no service to attend and leave. There was a room, a table, a meal, the Scriptures read aloud, prayers, and a few dozen people who knew one another and were learning to share a life. The historian Rodney Stark, studying how this movement actually grew, found that it spread not through mass persuasion but through networks of relationship, ordinary believers drawing their neighbors and kin into a community so thick with care that outsiders wanted in before they were fully convinced. The early church grew, Stark argued, because it was a superior community, not because it ran a superior campaign.

The earliest manual we possess shows a church that took formation with deadly seriousness. The Didache, the teaching of the twelve apostles, written perhaps within living memory of the apostles themselves, opens with the words there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and then walks the new believer through a whole way of living before it ever discusses worship. It assumes that becoming a Christian means being formed into a new kind of person inside a community that will hold you to it. Alan Kreider, in his study of the early church which he called the patient ferment, showed that the path into the church was long and demanding, often a catechumenate of years, in which a convert was not merely taught doctrine but apprenticed into a transformed life, watched, mentored, and changed before being baptized. The early church did not make consumers because it did not believe a person could be made a Christian in an afternoon. It believed a person had to be formed, slowly, in a body, and it was patient enough to do it.

Kreider's deepest insight cuts directly against everything we have built. The early church grew, he showed, not by being attractional but by being patient, not by improving its services but by producing people whose changed lives were themselves the argument. It did not advertise. It fermented. Its members were formed by habit and proximity into a people so distinct in how they loved their enemies, kept their marriages, freed their slaves, fed the poor, and faced their deaths that the watching pagan world was first baffled, then drawn. The conversion happened because the community was real, and the community was real because no one was a spectator. There was no way to be a member of that church and remain a stranger to it.

When the persecutions ended and the buildings came, the conviction was kept alive in the monastic movement, which built an entire way of life on the refusal to let the Christian be alone. Benedict, writing his Rule in the sixth century, ordered a common life in which monks ate together, worked together, prayed together, owned nothing privately, and submitted to one another and to a rule, on the conviction that a soul is formed not in isolation but in the friction and grace of a shared life. The cloister was a deliberate protest against the idea that a person could grow holy on his own. For fifteen centuries it preserved, in concentrated form, the early church's certainty that discipleship is communal or it is nothing.

And in the darkest century of the modern church, the insight returned with terrible clarity. In 1939, as the German church collapsed into compromise with the Nazi state, Dietrich Bonhoeffer gathered a small illegal seminary and wrote Life Together, a short book that reads like the early church remembered. The Christian, Bonhoeffer insisted, needs other Christians, not as an optional comfort but as a necessity, because the word of God comes to us most surely through the brother and sister, and the believer who tries to stand alone will fall. He warned against the wish-dream of an ideal community that loves its own vision of fellowship more than the actual, difficult people God has given, and he taught that real community is found only by those who lay down their fantasies and bear with one another in the flesh. Bonhoeffer wrote it as the consumer church of his own day was proving unable to resist evil, and he understood why. A faith with no real body has no spine. The recovery of disciple-making, he saw, is the recovery of life together, and we have been slow, eighty years later, to believe him.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The diagnosis of consumer faith did not come first from the church. It came in large part from sociologists and historians of American life who watched what individualism did to every institution, including ours, and a believer can receive their findings gratefully and critically at once, because all truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of why we became consumers carries a hidden picture of what a person is and what a person is for, and the picture is where the wisdom is won or lost.

secular.source: Habits of the Heart and the study of American individualism
secular.author: Robert Bellah and colleagues, 1985
secular.whatItGetsRight: Bellah and his team, interviewing ordinary Americans, found that the language of individualism had grown so total that people could no longer give an account of their commitments in any terms but personal preference. They met a woman they called Sheila, who named her private faith after herself, Sheilaism, a religion of one with her own small voice as its only authority. Bellah saw that this expressive individualism had hollowed out every community that depends on shared obligation, including the church, leaving people unable even to explain why they should belong to anything that asks something of them. He named with precision the disease the consumer church is dying of.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Bellah diagnoses the symptom with rare clarity and cannot reach the root, which Scripture names without flinching. Sheilaism is not merely a sociological drift. It is the ancient sin in a modern dress, the self enthroned as its own god, every man doing what is right in his own eyes, which the Bible treats as the mark of a people with no king. Bellah can describe the religion of the autonomous self. He cannot say what Scripture says, that the self was made to be ruled and is in rebellion, and that the cure is not better community technique but a crucified self raised into a body whose head is not me. The research names the captivity. Only the gospel breaks it.

secular.source: Democracy in America and the warning about individualism
secular.author: Alexis de Tocqueville, 1835
secular.whatItGetsRight: Tocqueville, traveling the young American republic, coined the word individualism and saw with prophetic clarity where it would lead. He described a society in which each citizen would draw apart into the small circle of family and friends, abandon the wider society to itself, and leave the public square to be filled by a soft and managing power. He warned that the equality and freedom Americans loved carried within them a tendency to isolate, to make every person forget his ancestors, hide his descendants, and shut himself up in the solitude of his own heart. He foresaw, a century and a half early, the lonely consumer the church would eventually be made of.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Tocqueville saw the trajectory and reached, wisely, for religion as the counterweight, but he saw it from the outside, as a useful brace for the republic. Scripture will not let the church be a civic medicine for loneliness. The body of Christ is not a remedy for American isolation that happens to work. It is the new humanity created by the cross, in which the dividing walls are broken down and strangers are made into one new people, citizens together of a kingdom that is not America. Tocqueville rightly fears the solitary heart and rightly looks to faith. He cannot name the deeper thing, that the church is not a tool for holding a nation together but the firstfruits of a world remade, and it heals isolation only because it first kills the isolated self and raises it into Christ.

secular.source: A Secular Age and the rise of the age of authenticity
secular.author: Charles Taylor
secular.whatItGetsRight: Taylor traced how the modern West came to live in what he called the age of authenticity, a moral world in which the highest good is to be true to your own unique inner self and to find your own way, free of any authority that would tell you what your life is for. He showed that this is now the water we swim in, shaping even the devout, so that faith itself becomes one more chosen path to personal fulfillment, held lightly and customized to taste. He explained, more deeply than anyone, why the modern Christian instinctively treats the church as a resource for the self rather than an authority over it.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Taylor maps the age of self-fashioning brilliantly and stops where the gospel begins its hardest work. The age of being true to yourself is the precise inversion of the call of Jesus, who said that whoever would find his life must lose it, and whoever would come after him must deny himself and take up a cross. Scripture does not offer the self a path to its own fulfillment. It announces the self's death and resurrection into Someone else's life. Taylor rightly shows that the modern believer wants a faith that serves the self. The gospel answers that the self that wants such a faith must die, and that the true self is found not by being expressed but by being crucified with Christ and hidden with him in God.

secular.source: Bowling Alone and the measure of social capital
secular.author: Robert Putnam
secular.whatItGetsRight: Putnam documented, with mountains of data, the steady collapse of American community across the second half of the twentieth century, the emptying of the clubs, the unions, the leagues, the dinner parties, and the churches, as Americans withdrew into private life. He showed that the decline was real, measurable, and costly, that a society starved of thick face-to-face belonging grows sicker, lonelier, and less able to trust. His work establishes beyond argument that the consumer who attends without belonging is not an isolated case but the product of a civilization-wide unraveling of shared life.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Putnam measures the loss precisely and reaches, like Tocqueville, for community as the cure while missing what makes the church's community unlike any club he counted. Scripture grounds Christian belonging not in the social benefits of connection but in a prior and astonishing fact, that God welcomed us into his own household while we were strangers and enemies, and made us members of one another by the blood of his Son. A community built only to cure loneliness will dissolve the moment the people in it become difficult, but a body grounded in having been welcomed by grace can keep bearing with the unbearable. Putnam names the crisis with care. The gospel supplies a belonging that does not depend on the members being lovable, because it did not begin with us being lovable.

secular.source: The McDonaldization of the church and the critique of the religious marketplace
secular.author: Sociologists of American religion in the consumer mode
secular.whatItGetsRight: A body of sociological work has shown how thoroughly American religion came to operate as a competitive marketplace, with churches as firms competing for religious consumers who shop among them for the best experience at the lowest cost of commitment. These scholars described the rationalization of faith into efficient, predictable, controllable products, the rise of the seeker who samples and the church that markets, and the way the whole logic trains believers to expect to receive rather than to belong. They named, in the cool language of social science, exactly the machinery that turned the body of Christ into a vendor and the disciple into a customer.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The marketplace analysis exposes the machinery accurately and cannot, on its own terms, condemn it, because it has no standard above the market by which to judge a market. Scripture supplies the standard. The church is not a firm and the believer is not a consumer, because the church is the bride and the body of Christ, bought at the price of his blood, and a bride cannot be comparison-shopped and a body cannot be assembled from satisfied customers. The sociology can show what we have become. Only the gospel can tell us it is a desecration, that to treat the blood-bought body of the Lord as a vendor of experiences is to profane a holy thing, and that the cure is not a better market position but repentance, and a return to being a body that belongs to its head and to one another.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who agree entirely that consumer faith is a counterfeit, and who long for the recovery of the disciple-making body, still differ on where the rebuilding should center, and the difference is not careless. It runs to whether the renewal of disciple-making should be pursued by reforming the gathered congregation we already have or by recovering the small, shared, household-scaled body the early church knew. Hear each view at its strongest, because the wisest pastors hold both in tension, and the difference is largely one of where to put the weight.

views.view: Reform the gathered church from within
views.body: This view holds that the answer to consumer faith is to reform the existing congregation rather than to abandon it, recovering depth inside the structures most Christians actually inhabit. It takes seriously that the gathered church, with its preaching, its sacraments, its ordained leadership, and its Sunday assembly, is the form the church has taken across most of its history, and that the New Testament itself shows the church gathering as a whole body to hear the word and break bread together. The danger is not the congregation. The danger is the consumer who haunts it, and the cure is to disciple that consumer back into a member, by preaching that calls for surrender rather than satisfaction, by membership that means covenant rather than attendance, by elders who actually shepherd named people, and by building the one-another life of the body inside the church through committed small groups, real accountability, and a recovered church discipline. Advocates argue that to write off the gathered congregation is to throw away the very structures that have carried the faith for two thousand years, the ordered ministry of word and sacrament that no living-room gathering can fully replace, and that the renewal of the church has nearly always come not from leaving the institution but from reforming it from the inside. The failure they are guarding against is real, a restless and prideful spirit that despises the ordinary church, is forever leaving to find something purer, and ends up accountable to no one, having mistaken its own consumer impulse for a prophetic one. They are quick to add that reform which never produces real, known, burden-bearing community has not reformed anything, and that a large church full of strangers, however orthodox its preaching, has not yet recovered the body the New Testament describes.

views.view: Recover the small and shared household body
views.body: This view holds that the answer to consumer faith is to recover the small, shared, household-scaled body the early church actually was, because the consumer is in large part a creature of scale, and certain things simply cannot happen in a crowd. It takes seriously that for its first three centuries the church met in homes, that its life ran on tables and proximity and a few dozen people who knew one another, and that the one-another commands assume a body small enough for everyone to be known. The danger, on this reading, is not merely the consumer's heart but the structures that manufacture consumers, the platform that creates an audience, the scale that guarantees anonymity, the production that trains people to receive. The cure is to rebuild the church from the household up, in homes and around tables, in small communities where no one can hide, where the ordinary believer is the minister, and where formation happens through a genuinely shared life rather than a delivered service. Advocates argue that we have tried for generations to reform the large gathering into a place of deep formation and have mostly produced better-attended anonymity, and that the early church's astonishing power was inseparable from its small and shared form. The failure they are guarding against is real, a church that improves its preaching and its programs while leaving untouched the very scale and structure that made consumers of its people in the first place. They are quick to add that the household church must not curdle into a private and isolated cell, that the New Testament households were knit into the wider body of the city and the apostles, and that a small community which severs itself from the church catholic has traded one error for another.

parts.title: What Belonging Forms That Consuming Cannot
parts.body:
Consumer faith forms a person too, and this is the part we miss. It does not leave you neutral while it fails to disciple you. It disciples you into a consumer, trains you week by week in the posture of evaluation and detachment, and forms in you exactly the self that cannot be formed into Christ. To leave it is not merely to change your schedule. It is to let God form in you the things the body produces and the crowd never can, and most of them will cost you something before they bless you.

Belonging forms the death of the sovereign self, which is the one thing the age of self-expression cannot abide and the one thing the gospel requires. The consumer keeps final authority over his own life, sampling the church as he samples everything, retaining the right to leave the moment it asks more than he wishes to give. To belong to a body is to surrender that authority, to bind yourself to people you did not choose and cannot return, to let them have a real claim on your time, your home, your money, and your sin. This feels like a loss, and it is, and it is the loss Jesus called the only road to life. The self that dies in the body is the false self that was killing you, and the self that rises is the one that can finally be known and loved.

It forms the patience to bear with real people, which the wish-dream of an ideal community always destroys. Bonhoeffer saw it exactly. Those who love their dream of community more than the community itself will wreck every actual fellowship they enter, because real people are disappointing, and a body is made of real people. Belonging sands away the romance until what is left is the love that actually saves, the patient, particular, inconvenient love that keeps showing up for the brother who irritates you and the sister who wounded you. You learn in the body that you are far more selfish than you believed, far quicker to leave, far more of a consumer in your own heart than you ever admitted, and that learning is not the body failing you. It is the body forming you.

It forms a Christian who can be corrected, which the consumer, accountable to no one, can never become. In the crowd you can sit for thirty years and never once be told the truth about yourself, because no one is close enough to see it and you have arranged it that way. In the body there are people who know your patterns, who love you enough to name the sin you cannot see, and who have earned the right to be heard. This is brutal and it is mercy. A faith that has no one in it who can tell you no is a faith curving steadily toward the self, and the slow, humbling grace of being known and corrected by people who stay is one of the surest signs that you are being made into a disciple rather than catered to as a customer.

And belonging forms in you, at last, an understanding of the gospel from the inside, because the body is the gospel made visible. The God who saved you did not save you into a private arrangement. He saved you into a people, made you a member of a household, joined you to a body whose head is his Son, and every time you bear a burden you did not have to bear, welcome a stranger into your home, confess a sin to a brother, or stay in a community you wanted to leave, you are living out in miniature the very thing God did for you, who bore your burden, welcomed you when you were a stranger, and would not leave. You cannot keep practicing the one-another life without being changed by it, without the love you are learning to give teaching you, slowly, how astonishing was the love you were given. That is the secret the consumer never finds. While you are giving your life away to a body you did not choose, the God who gave his life for a body of enemies is making a disciple of you.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: This is the part the whole resource exists for, because consumer faith is not a position to argue against but a habit to be walked out of, and almost anyone can begin the walk. You do not need to plant a church or burn down the one you attend. You need to stop attending alone, let yourself be known by a few people, take up the one-another life, and begin sharing your life with others rather than consuming a service near them. What follows is a concrete path from your first honest step out of the crowd toward a reproducing, disciple-making body. Begin this week, with one move toward being known.

steps: Name your own consumer patterns honestly before God, on paper. Write down how you actually relate to your church. Do you attend without belonging, evaluate without committing, receive without giving, remain unknown by design. Repentance begins where the consumer is named, and it begins with me, not with the church I am tempted to blame.

Reach toward one person to begin being known. Ask one believer to coffee and tell them something true about your actual life, a struggle, a question, a fear, the thing you usually keep behind the handshake. The whole road out of consumer faith starts with the decision to let one person past the surface.

Stop comparison-shopping your church for a season and ask a different question. Not what am I getting here, but who here could I begin to belong to, and what does this body need from me. Change the question and you have already begun to change the posture.

Open your home once this week. Invite one or two people from your church to a simple meal, no agenda, just the beginning of a shared life. The body has always been built at tables, and a single open evening is a larger step out of consumer faith than a year of better attendance.

Commit to a small enough body that you can actually be known, and show up relentlessly. Join the group, the class, the few, whatever your church offers that is small enough for the one-another life, and protect that gathering like a bill that must be paid. Formation is the fruit of proximity over time, and proximity requires showing up when you do not feel like it.

Begin practicing one of the one-another commands on purpose. Pick one, bear one another's burdens, confess to one another, encourage one another, and do it deliberately this month with a real person. Carry an actual burden. Speak an actual encouragement. The commands are not concepts to admire but practices to begin.

Move one relationship from friendly to known by letting someone in on your sin. Tell a trusted believer something you are ashamed of and ask them to walk with you in it. Nothing breaks the consumer's anonymity faster than confession, and nothing the church does forms a disciple more surely than being known at the worst point and loved anyway.

Give something the consumer withholds. Offer your time, your home, your money, or your hands to the body in a way that costs you and asks nothing back. The consumer receives. The member gives, and the giving is itself the medicine, because it trains the heart out of the posture of the customer.

Build a regular table into your life as the center of a shared body. Set a recurring meal in your home with the same handful of people, and let it grow over the season into a place where you eat, open Scripture, pray, and carry one another's lives. The household table is where the early church made disciples, and it is available to you now.

Let the body have real authority over you. Tell the few who know you that you want to be told the truth about yourself, and then receive correction without defending yourself when it comes. A Christian who cannot be corrected is a consumer in disguise, and a season of deliberately submitting to the loving honesty of others is a season of becoming a disciple.

Bear a costly burden with someone for the long haul. Find the person in your body who is suffering, the grief, the illness, the wayward child, the unraveling marriage, and commit to walk with them through it, not for a week but for as long as it takes. The one-another life is learned in the burdens that do not resolve quickly, and the carrying will form you as much as it helps them.

Begin to disciple someone, however ordinary you feel. Take a newer believer, a seeker, or a wandering friend, and start sharing your actual Christian life with them over meals and time, reading Scripture together, praying, letting them watch a real disciple live. You do not need training. You need to give away what you have, and the giving is how an attender becomes a maker of disciples.

Aim everything at reproduction from the start, so the body you are building is one that makes disciples who make disciples. Tell the people you are walking with, plainly, that they are being formed in order to form others, that the open chair and the shared life and the one-another love are theirs to give away. A disciple who is only ever fed becomes a consumer. A disciple who knows they are being equipped to feed others becomes a builder of the body.

Help start new tables and new communities rather than enlarging your own. When your shared body grows, resist the pull to keep everyone, and instead send people out to begin households and tables of their own, so that one shared life multiplies into many. The goal is not the biggest possible group but the most reproducing ones, until a neighborhood is threaded with bodies that know one another.

Work to reshape your wider church toward the body it is meant to be, from wherever you stand. You may not lead it, but you can be living proof within it, a member who belongs deeply, who shows others what the one-another life looks like, who quietly pulls people out of the crowd and into a body. Renewal almost always begins with a few who simply start living the real thing where they are.

Settle in for the long, unhurried, unglamorous work of being the church, through the seasons when the body is rich and the seasons when it is thin, trusting God with a harvest you cannot force. Some you welcome will be formed and some will drift, some communities will flourish and some will fade, and your task is not to control the outcome but to keep belonging, keep bearing, keep sharing the life, keep setting the table, the way the church has done since the upper room, until the day the whole body of Christ from every nation sits down together at the only table that finally matters, the feast of the Lamb that has no end.
